source: David Deamer, Deleuze's Cinema Books: Three Introductions to the Taxonomy of Images (Edinburgh UP, 2016); page numbers are printed page numbers (form-feed index − 35, verified against running heads)

legend.INFERENCE: our extrapolation, not in the text
legend.Marginal: sound mentioned only descriptively in a film reading, no theoretical link

key_finding: Deamer never builds a sound taxonomy of his own. He (1) pairs every opsign with a sonsign without differentiating them, (2) outsources the theory of film sound to Michel Chion (pp.167-168), placed inside the lectosign chapter, and (3) omits Cinema 2 ch.9 almost entirely (no speech acts, heautonomy, sound out-of-field, musical act, fabulation). Sound dimensions for the 45 elements come mostly from his Section III film readings.

passages.topic: sound in Bergson's matter-universe
passages.paraphrase: In the Bergsonian ground of the book, perception is interaction in matter: sound waves on the eardrum constitute an auditory image just as light on the retina constitutes a visual one. Sound is image from the outset, not a supplement.
passages.short_quote: describing an auditory image

passages.topic: both regimes are made of visual AND sound images
passages.paraphrase: Cinema transmits visual and sound images; both movement-images and time-images are necessarily composed of actual visual and sound images. The regimes differ in how they link these images, not in what materials they use.
passages.short_quote: actual visual and sound images of matter in space as movement

passages.topic: solid perception includes hearing
passages.paraphrase: The perception-image forms a solid subject by following a character and by seeing and hearing with that character. Point-of-audition is folded into point-of-view.
passages.short_quote: seeing and hearing with that character

passages.topic: sound as a disruptive element in the time-image
passages.paraphrase: In the time-image the film comes apart: sound and colour stop serving the flow and become disruptive in their own right, alongside intervals, caesuras and repetitions.
passages.short_quote: sound and colour become disruptive elements

passages.topic: musical analogy for the series of time
passages.paraphrase: Deamer compares the serial organisation of the powers of the false to serialism in music, which overturns traditional harmony by continually rearranging its basic elements. It is an analogy for chronosign structure, not a statement about film sound.
passages.short_quote: As in serialism in music

passages.topic: opsigns/sonsigns as zeroness; lectosign reads the sound image
passages.paraphrase: Opsigns and sonsigns are the actual visual and auditory images left once the movement-image's coordinates collapse (the '0' of the time-image table). Unlike hyalosigns, chronosigns and noosigns, they do not break down into three sub-signs. The lectosign is the limit that forces the optical AND the sound image to be read (citing C2: 24).
passages.short_quote: to treat the optical and sound image like something that is also readable

passages.topic: cinema of the brain includes the sounds of the world
passages.paraphrase: The third noosign does not depend on the actor's body but on the mise-en-scène: backgrounds, lighting, colours and sounds of the film-world as a brain-world.
passages.short_quote: the lighting, the colours and sounds of the world of the film

passages.topic: any-space-whatever becomes opsign-sonsign
passages.paraphrase: Quoting C2: 5, a pure optical or sound situation is set in an any-space-whatever. Once cut loose from the movement-image, the any-space-whatever becomes an opsign-sonsign, a de-differenciated visual and audio image (Four Times: the purest of sonsigns).
passages.short_quote: a purely optical or sound situation becomes established

passages.topic: sound as one of five disruptive practices
passages.paraphrase: The processes that create time-image cinema are listed as disruptive practices of framing, the shot, montage, sound and colour. Sound is one of five technical coordinates.
passages.short_quote: framing, the shot, montage, sound and colour

passages.topic: musicals as movement of world
passages.paraphrase: Under the implied dream (movement of world), worlds of pure imagination include musicals and dance films, where song and dance are natural to the film-world. This is the one place in Section II where a movement-image sign is tied to a sound form.
passages.short_quote: where the song and dance are a natural aspect of the real world

passages.topic: reverb-sound marks the flashback
passages.paraphrase: Strong destiny's flashback is marked by monochrome, slow motion or reverb on the sound. The audio treatment is one of the conventional signals that tell the viewer a recollection has begun.
passages.short_quote: reverb-sound

passages.topic: opsigns and sonsigns chapter
passages.paraphrase: The time-image begins with pure optical and sound situations produced by three ungroundings: stymied perception, the crisis of the action-image and the delinking of the movement-image. Deamer always treats opsign and sonsign jointly. He gives the sonsign no separate definition, examples or sub-types. Both are 'actual' images that open onto virtual correlates.
passages.short_quote: actual on-screen de-differenciated visual and audio images

passages.topic: movement-image = linkage of visual and sound image; out-of-field as virtual
passages.paraphrase: Actual images are the on-screen visuals and their accompanying audio. The movement-image works through actual-to-actual flow, including the linkage of visual image and sound image, and this flow effaces the virtual. Out-of-field and editing are where virtual connections can arise.
passages.short_quote: the linkage of visual and sound image

passages.topic: sonsigns are immediately hyalosigns
passages.paraphrase: Opsigns and sonsigns are visual and sonic fragments that immediately become hyalosigns, linking an actual image to its virtual in the present, the passing past or the coming future. Deamer does not say what a sound crystal would be.
passages.short_quote: visual and sonic fragments in a state of zeroness

passages.topic: two out-of-fields (relative vs absolute)
passages.paraphrase: Among Deleuze's five aspects of framing, the out-of-field matters most. One out-of-field is continuous and closed, like a glance off-screen or the rest of a body. The other subsists within the frame and opens onto the Open/virtual. Deamer frames this entirely in VISUAL terms here and does not use the words relative/absolute. Tying it to off-screen sound is our inference, supported only by p.168 (removing sound effects reduces the spatial out-of-field).
passages.short_quote: a more radical Elsewhere, outside homogenous space and time

passages.topic: the talkie: sound as a component of the visual image
passages.paraphrase: For Deleuze (per Deamer), the coming of sound moved music from the pit and speech from intertitles onto the optical track, and this strengthened realism. In the movement-image, sound becomes a new dimension or component of the visual image (C2: 226). Deamer traces this to Michel Chion.
passages.short_quote: a new dimension of the visual image, a new component

passages.topic: Chion's first schema: on-screen / off-screen (acousmatic) / nondiegetic
passages.paraphrase: Chion's first division has three terms. On-screen sound comes from a source in the image. Off-screen sound is acousmatic, heard without its cause being seen. Nondiegetic sound (music, voice-over) lies outside the film-world. The schema is unstable, because sounds can move between the categories, for example a voice-over later assigned to a character.
passages.short_quote: sounds one hears without seeing their originating cause

passages.topic: Chion's second schema: ambient / internal / on-the-air
passages.paraphrase: Chion's refinement adds three more. Ambient 'territory' sound, such as traffic or birds, never raises the question of its source. Internal sound comes from a character and is either objective (breathing) or subjective (voiced thought). On-the-air sound comes through radios and telephones and can enter or leave the image.
passages.short_quote: territory-sound

passages.topic: no soundtrack; synchresis; vertical vs horizontal
passages.paraphrase: Chion holds that there is no soundtrack running parallel to the image. The audiovisual relation is a contract, not a natural harmony, and it works vertically: synchresis welds a sound to a visible event, as a voice is tied to a moving face. Deleuze picks this up for the movement-image: sound components are separate only in the abstraction of pure hearing, and together they form a fourth dimension of the visual image, a single continuum (C2: 235).
passages.short_quote: fourth dimension of the visual image

passages.topic: how the time-image breaks the audiovisual contract
passages.paraphrase: Chion's tactics of disruption are these: suppress music that reinforces affect or action, remove sound effects (which shrinks the spatial out-of-field), and denaturalise the voice through theatrical speech, textual speech (the voice overloads the image), decentering (the image overloads the voice), or foreign languages without subtitles. These tactics expose the contract rather than achieving a 'true' disjunction, and doing so creates the time-image.
passages.short_quote: expose the audiovisual contract and create the time-image

passages.topic: all five coordinates attacked
passages.paraphrase: In the lectosign's summary, frame, shot, montage, colour and sound are all attacked and destroyed. From this zeroness hyalosigns, chronosigns and noosigns are built, and a film must then be read.
passages.short_quote: Frame, shot, montage, colour and sound

passages.topic: Diving Bell: solid perception in the sound field
passages.paraphrase: Identification is total in the sound field as well as visually. We hear others' words and Jean-Do's thoughts as voice-over, the voice of a body not yet seen. The film opens on black, silence and breathing, with the doctor's voice arriving in waves.
passages.short_quote: Not only visually, but also in the sound field

passages.topic: Timecode: audio as the 'fourth flow' of liquid perception
passages.paraphrase: Audio (music, voice, effects) is one of the flows of liquid perception. Jazz refrains cover the whole field and bind the four quadrants. The voices and effects of one quadrant are brought up while the other three go quiet, which guides the eye without fixing it. Figgis mixed the sound live, so each screening differed.
passages.short_quote: Fourth flow: the audio element – music, voice, sound effects.

passages.topic: Naqoyqatsi: gaseous perception through music-images
passages.paraphrase: Thousands of disparate images vary with and against Philip Glass's music-images. The film is organised into nine movements, each with its own music-image trajectory. Chant and heartbeat drums open it.
passages.short_quote: music-images of Philip Glass

passages.topic: The Terrorist: the icon's near-silence
passages.paraphrase: Close-ups of the face that last a 'little eternity' come close to silence, leaving only breathing and ambient nature, or else a score of synthetic strings swamps them.
passages.short_quote: approach silence, except for her breathing

passages.topic: Human Centipede: silence as reception
passages.paraphrase: This is about the audience, not the soundtrack. Laughter in the screening room drowns the victim's muffled screams until the shot is held too long and a painful silence falls. The symptom is registered in the hall's sound.
passages.short_quote: the screening room discovers a painful silence

passages.topic: Killer Inside Me: restrained sound
passages.paraphrase: Frame, shot, editing, colour and sound are restrained and realist, with no jagged music, so the style mirrors Lou's composure.
passages.short_quote: no jagged musical accompaniment

passages.topic: Wandering Cloud: song-and-dance as plastic figure
passages.paraphrase: Stretches with almost no dialogue are broken by vivid musical numbers (sixties Chinese pop). These do not grow out of the day-to-day world but rupture it, and Deamer calls them plastic figures par excellence.
passages.short_quote: plastic figures par excellence

passages.topic: Scott Pilgrim: sound rendered as graphics
passages.paraphrase: Sound is drawn on screen as comic-book graphics, and the soundtrack interweaves music fragments with cartoon effects. These belong to the theatrical figure's code.
passages.short_quote: music fragments and cartoonish sound-effects

passages.topic: Slackistan: reflexive voice-over, quoted sound
passages.paraphrase: Hasan's voice-over comments with a reflexive omniscience. A ceiling fan is overdubbed with a helicopter, quoting Apocalypse Now. Dialogue echoes Breathless and Pulp Fiction, and English and Urdu interweave.
passages.short_quote: reflexive omniscience of the voice-over

passages.topic: A Screaming Man: quotidian sound
passages.paraphrase: The camera lingers in silences broken only by a scratching pen. Diegetic sound prevails, the actors speak sotto voce, and the war is at first only background noise. An unheard answer works as an ellipsis.
passages.short_quote: diegetic sound prevails

passages.topic: Buried: audio-visual economy, voices at a distance
passages.paraphrase: The film opens with no image and no articulate language: black, breathing, shouting. All action happens off-screen, and rescuers, insurgents and family exist only as distant voices on the phone.
passages.short_quote: no image, no articulate language

passages.topic: Five: the sonsign in practice
passages.paraphrase: The old men's talk is never heard, only the roar of the waves. The first four sequences are soaked in the sea's white noise. The last begins in near silence on black, then a chorus of toads and a storm swell into the roar of nature. Everything, sound included, is undone, and this crisis creates opsigns and sonsigns.
passages.short_quote: All we hear is the roar of the breaking waves.

passages.topic: Uncle Boonmee: voice-over over photogrammes
passages.paraphrase: The dream of the future is narrated by Boonmee in voice-over over still, contemporary photogrammes. The voice and the image belong to different times.
passages.short_quote: narrated in voice-over by Boonmee

passages.topic: Russian Ark: sound never fully apprehended
passages.paraphrase: Peter the Great's voices are heard at a distance through dark glass and old stone. The camera tries for a better visual and sound grasp and never gets it.
passages.short_quote: attempting to achieve a better visual and sound apprehension

passages.topic: Police, Adjective: language, song, no emotive music
passages.paraphrase: Language is central. A pop song's words are meaningless to Cristi but poetry to his wife, the dictionary scene turns on words, and the denouement refuses emotive music. Deamer frames this as bodies of gest, minor cinema and collective enunciation (via Kafka, p.332).
passages.short_quote: words used as poetry

passages.topic: Dogville: narrator's voice and invisible-object foley as noosign
passages.paraphrase: Doors that do not exist creak and knocks sound on invisible walls. The narrator's voice stays in the sound field, explaining and warning. These sound images expose how world, bodies and objects are linked, make the storytelling function visible, and force a reading.
passages.short_quote: the soundscape of the narrator’s voice and invisible objects

passages.topic: Enter the Void: lectosign voice
passages.paraphrase: Oscar's speech and thought share one blank voice-over, which makes their status undecidable. The trip's sonics are whispers, blank voices and uterine soundscapes. The film is an exemplary lectosign.
passages.short_quote: making the status of speech and thought indeterminate

passages.topic: WHAT DEAMER DOES NOT COVER
passages.paraphrase: The text contains no occurrences of: talkie, speech act / speech-act, reflexive / interactive / storytelling speech acts (as a typology), heautonomy, audio-visual image (as Deleuze's C2 ch.9 concept), sound out-of-field in the relative/absolute sense, free indirect discourse, fabulation, legending, the musical sign, or voice-off in Deleuze's sense. 'Refrain' appears once, as a word for jazz themes in Timecode (p.184), not the D&G concept. The only C2 ch.9 citations are C2: 226 and C2: 235 (both via Chion) and C2: 245 (reading). Deamer replaces Deleuze's ch.9 sound theory with Chion's typology.

components.name: On-screen sound
components.definition: Sound whose source is visible in the frame, e.g. a band playing in shot.

components.name: Off-screen (acousmatic) sound
components.definition: Sound heard without its cause being seen. It can later be visualised (de-acousmatised), or the reverse can happen.

components.name: Nondiegetic sound
components.definition: Sound outside the film-world: score music, voice-over narration. The boundary is unstable (a voice-over may turn out to be a character's).

components.name: Ambient / territory sound
components.definition: Continuous background such as traffic or birdsong that never raises the question of its source. It establishes a place.

components.name: Internal sound (objective / subjective)
components.definition: Sound from inside a character: objective (breathing, heartbeat) or subjective (voiced thought).

components.name: On-the-air sound
components.definition: Sound through a device (radio, telephone, TV) that can pass into or out of the image.

components.name: Synchresis (vertical relation)
components.definition: The welding of a sound to a simultaneous visible event, e.g. voice to lips. It makes the relation vertical (harmonic) rather than a parallel horizontal track, so sound becomes a 'fourth dimension' of the visual image in the movement-image.

components.name: Audiovisual contract
components.definition: The relation of sound and image is conventional, not natural. The time-image does not achieve a 'pure' disjunction; it exposes the contract.

components.name: Music (reinforcing affect/action)
components.definition: In the talkie, music moved from the orchestra pit onto the track. In the movement-image it reinforces affection or action; suppressing it is a time-image tactic.

components.name: Speech (from intertitle to track)
components.definition: In the talkie, speech that had been intertitles (or a live narrator) moved onto the optical track, strengthening realism.

components.name: Sound effects
components.definition: Noises tied to visible events. Removing them shrinks the spatial out-of-field; in Timecode they spotlight one zone of the frame.

components.name: Denaturalised voice: theatrical speech
components.definition: Speech delivered as performance rather than naturalistic talk.

components.name: Denaturalised voice: textual speech
components.definition: The voice overloads the visual image: text dominates what is seen.

components.name: Denaturalised voice: decentering
components.definition: The visual image overloads the sound image: speech is swamped or sidelined.

components.name: Denaturalised voice: foreign language unsubtitled
components.definition: Speech heard as sound, not meaning.

components.name: Sonsign (pure sound situation)
components.definition: The actual sound image cut off from its motor extension. It belongs to the zeroness of the time-image, is jointly defined with the opsign, and immediately becomes a hyalosign (sound fragment + virtual). Deamer gives no sub-types.

components.name: Readable sound image (lectosign)
components.definition: In the time-image the sound image, like the optical one, must be read rather than simply heard.

components.name: Silence
components.definition: Not given a theoretical role. In the Section III readings it recurs as the ground of the icon's close-up, the quotidian, and the sonsign's black screen.

components.name: Voice-over
components.source: Deamer's film readings (not theorised beyond Chion's nondiegetic)
components.definition: Across the readings it works as subjective thought (Diving Bell), reflexive omniscience (Slackistan), a voice from another time (Boonmee), a narrator exposing storytelling (Dogville), and speech/thought made indistinct (Enter the Void).

element_sound.name: Solid perception
element_sound.sound: TEXT: hearing with the character (p.13). Diving Bell: identification extends into the sound field, with the protagonist's thoughts as voice-over, breathing, and voices arriving in waves (pp.179-180). Internal subjective sound = point-of-audition anchored in one body.

element_sound.name: Liquid perception
element_sound.sound: TEXT: Timecode, the audio 'fourth flow' (p.184). Music covers all zones while a mix spotlights one quadrant's voices and effects, so the centre is handed off by sound.

element_sound.name: Gaseous perception
element_sound.sound: TEXT: Naqoyqatsi (pp.186-188). Images vary against Glass's 'music-images' in nine movements; the sound has no human centre.

element_sound.name: Icon
element_sound.sound: TEXT (Section III only): The Terrorist's close-ups approach silence with only breathing and ambient nature, or are swamped by synthetic strings (pp.189-190). Section II gives the affection-image no sound dimension.

element_sound.name: Any-space-whatever
element_sound.sound: TEXT: a pure optical OR SOUND situation is set in an any-space-whatever (C2: 5, p.60). Freed from the movement-image, the any-space-whatever becomes an opsign-sonsign (pp.86, 197-198: Four Times, 'purest of sonsigns'). Sounds are not specified.

element_sound.name: Symptom
element_sound.sound: TEXT (reception only): Human Centipede, where audience laughter drowns the screams and then a painful silence falls in the screening room (pp.202-204). Nothing about the film's own soundtrack.

element_sound.name: Originary world
element_sound.sound: TEXT (descriptive only): Innocence, with night-time noises echoing in the woods and disembodied voices ('a voice growls') (pp.210-211). Not theorised.

element_sound.name: Index of lack
element_sound.sound: TEXT (descriptive only): Mother opens on wind in grass, then tablas, guitar and strings as the woman dances 'to music only she can hear' (pp.213-214). Not theorised.

element_sound.name: Index of equivocity
element_sound.sound: TEXT (descriptive only): Killer Inside Me's sound is restrained and realist, with 'no jagged musical accompaniment', mirroring Lou (p.218).

element_sound.name: Binomial
element_sound.sound: Marginal: a silent, empty shop floor opens Made in Dagenham (p.228). No theory.

element_sound.name: Imprint
element_sound.sound: Marginal: a song ('California Dreaming') functions as a narrative object in Fish Tank (p.237). No theory.

element_sound.name: Plastic figure
element_sound.sound: TEXT: Wandering Cloud's song-and-dance numbers rupture a near-silent everyday world and are 'plastic figures par excellence' (pp.238-240).

element_sound.name: Theatrical figure
element_sound.sound: TEXT (descriptive): Scott Pilgrim renders sound as graphics and its soundtrack interweaves music fragments with cartoon effects (pp.242-243).

element_sound.name: Mise en abyme
element_sound.sound: Marginal: 'unending silent laughter' of passengers in Source Code (p.244). No sound theory.

element_sound.name: Figure of enfeeblement
element_sound.sound: TEXT (descriptive): Slackistan's voice-over has 'reflexive omniscience'. A fan is overdubbed with a helicopter quoting Apocalypse Now, dialogue echoes other films, and Urdu/English interweave (p.252).

element_sound.name: Quotidian
element_sound.sound: TEXT (descriptive): A Screaming Man, with lingering silences, a pen scratching, 'diegetic sound prevails', sotto voce acting, war as background noise, and an unheard answer as ellipsis (pp.255-256).

element_sound.name: Limit of the large form action-image
element_sound.sound: Marginal/plot: in Monsters the sound of planes draws the creatures out (p.260). No theory.

element_sound.name: Limit of the small form action-image
Rich dream
element_sound.sound: Marginal: Star Trek, with a woman's voice at the edge of consciousness and a whisper (p.269). No theory.

element_sound.name: Movement of world
element_sound.sound: TEXT (Section II): musicals and dance films, where song and dance are natural to the world, are cases of the implied dream (p.125).

element_sound.name: Strong destiny
element_sound.sound: TEXT (Section II): the flashback is signalled by 'reverb-sound', along with monochrome and slow motion (p.128). Section III adds a door that 'whispers' and a silent entrance (p.275).

element_sound.name: Symbol
element_sound.sound: TEXT (Section III): Buried is an audio-visual economy of 'no image, no articulate language'. Action is off-screen and the others are 'voices at a distance' on the phone (pp.294-295). This is the only reading where off-screen (acousmatic) sound carries a whole film. Section II gives the relation-image no sound dimension.

element_sound.name: Opsign
element_sound.sound: TEXT: always paired with the sonsign as 'visual and audio' de-differenciated images (pp.138, 143, 162). The opsign has no sound dimension of its own; its twin is 34b.

element_sound.name: Sonsign
element_sound.sound: TEXT: pure actual sound situation, the actual sound image cut off from motor extension (pp.41-45, 138-145, 162). Deamer gives no separate definition, examples or sub-types. Five supplies the practice: talk swallowed by the waves' roar, the sea's white noise, near silence, the toads' crescendo (pp.302, 304). Chion's tactics (p.168) are Deamer's only account of HOW sound becomes time-image.

element_sound.name: Limpid and opaque
element_sound.sound: Marginal: in Self Made the shift in production form includes its sound (p.311). No theory. Section II says only that sonsigns become hyalosigns (pp.145, 149).

element_sound.name: Peaks of the present
element_sound.sound: TEXT (descriptive): Uncle Boonmee's future-dream is narrated in voice-over over still photogrammes, so voice and image are out of time with each other (p.318).

element_sound.name: Sheets of the past
element_sound.sound: TEXT (descriptive): Russian Ark, with voices heard at a distance and sound obscured by glass and stone. The camera never achieves 'visual and sound apprehension' (p.322).

element_sound.name: Powers of the false
element_sound.sound: Analogy only: the series of time is likened to serialism in music (p.44). Nothing on film sound.

element_sound.name: Bodies of attitude
element_sound.sound: Marginal: Dylan as singer; folk and gospel as story content in I'm Not There (pp.328-329). No theory.

element_sound.name: Bodies of gest
element_sound.sound: TEXT (descriptive): Police, Adjective, where language is central, a pop song is meaningless words vs 'poetry', the dictionary scene, and the denouement refuses emotive music (pp.330-332).

element_sound.name: Cinema of the brain
element_sound.sound: TEXT: the noosign's mise-en-scène includes the 'sounds of the world of the film' (pp.56, 159). Dogville: the narrator's voice plus foley for invisible objects exposes the storytelling function (pp.335-336).

element_sound.name: Lectosigns
element_sound.sound: TEXT: the optical AND sound image must be read (C2: 24, p.45). Sound is one of the five coordinates attacked (pp.163, 171). Chion's synchresis and contract are discussed here (pp.167-168). Enter the Void: one blank voice-over for speech and thought; 'whispers, blank voices, uterine soundscapes' (pp.338, 342).

axes.note: The most solidly grounded axis. Deamer notes sounds can travel between the cells, which could be a table mechanic.

axes.grounding: TEXT: Chion's second schema plus the talkie triad, pp.167-168
axes.note: The rows of a mixing desk.

values: synchresis (sound as 4th dimension of visual image; movement-image)
axes.note: Deamer's only regime-level claim about sound.
These can be operators in the mixing engine: applying one pushes a mix toward the sonsign/time-image side.
A continuous slider derived from two of Chion's tactics.

axes.grounding: TEXT: pp.41-46, 68, 144, 171 (the sound side of the same series)
axes.note: Deamer gives the series but no sound-specific content for 1-3; the sound cells would be INFERENCE, with Section III readings as anchors (Russian Ark 39, Boonmee 38, Dogville 43, Enter the Void 44).

axes.grounding: INFERENCE from pp.13, 139 + Section III readings pp.179-188
axes.note: Deamer never states a sound version of this axis. His three perception readings (Naqoyqatsi / Timecode / Diving Bell) all describe sound in a way that maps onto it.

values: absolute: sound that subsists in the frame, opening onto the virtual
axes.grounding: TEXT for the visual frame (p.164). Application to sound is INFERENCE, supported by p.168's link between effects and the spatial out-of-field and Buried pp.294-295
axes.note: Deamer does not use Deleuze's sound out-of-field or the relative/absolute terms.

axes.grounding: INFERENCE, extending the frame's saturation/rarefaction (p.163) to sound; silence recurs in readings pp.179, 189, 255, 304
